chunks.text: Semantic Feedback-Based RAG for Radiology Report Generation Xing Jia, Yun Xiong*, Songwen Pei, Yumeng Zhang, Cairong Yan, and Zhijun Fang Abstract: Radiology report generation aims to produce textual reports automatically based on input images, a critical process that aids in accurate diagnoses and lightens the workload of radiologists. Following recent advances in Large Language Models (LLMs), several Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG) based report generation models have been proposed. Despite the continuously improved performance, these report generation models often suffer from two main limitations, i.e., interference of irrelevant information, and lack of alignment between the input image and the resulting generated report. In this study, we propose the Semantic feedback based RAG Radiology report generation model, namely RAGSemRad. RAGSemRad comprises two key components: the fine-grained semantic retrieval module and the semantic assessment module. The fine- grained semantic retrieval module is designed to retrieve adequate and relevant prompt information, while ignoring irrelevant interference. This is achieved by clustering the data at the semantic level and leveraging the domain knowledge within a large pre-trained visual-language model, thus alleviating the issues of hallucination and databias. Further, the semantic assessment module enhances the performance of the upper bound by enhancing the alignment between the input image and the resulting generated report, utilizing supervision signals derived from paired image-label data. Experimental evaluations are conducted on two benchmarks, IU X-Ray and MIMIC-CXR, to assess the performance of RAGSemRad. The results demonstrate RAGSemRad exhibits competitive performance compared to the state-of-the-art methods, showcasing its potential to advance automatic radiology report generation. In recent years, there has been a surge of interest in report generation methods, inspired by tasks such as image captioning[2] and paragraph generation[3]. A number of methods have been proposed for report generation, as evidenced by a wide range of studies[1, 4–19]. These methods have significantly advanced the field of report generation in the medical domain. The prevailing methods for generating reports typically adhere to the encoder-decoder framework, originally tailored for neural machine translation[20]. In this framework, Convolutional Neural Networks (CNNs) are often employed as encoders to extract intricate feature representations from input images. Subsequently, decoders, such as Recurrent Neural Networks (RNNs) or Transformers, are utilized to transform these feature representations into textual reports. The main difference between image captioning (or paragraph generation) and report generation is that report generation pays more attention to the fundamental concern of clinical accuracy, i.e., the alignment between the input image and the resulting generated report. As show in Fig. 1, the clinical accuracy of the sentence “heart size in normal” is bad, since the ground-truth is “heart size in enlarged”. Moreover, in the context of report generation, it is essential to emphasize abnormalities or diseases that are critical for assisting radiologists in making informed clinical decisions. In other words, for a high- quality report, above all, it needs to be semantically correct. Furthermore, it should highlight abnormalities or diseases. Existing methods in radiology report generation primarily focus on optimizing applying text-similarity objectives, such as teacher-forcing or reinforcement learning. However, text-similarity-driven strategies tend to result in generated reports with low clinical accuracy. Current RAG-based report generation methods typically retrieve the entire report or only the summary content (i.e., the “impression” part shown in Fig. 1) during the retrieval phase, thereby being interfered by irrelevant or inadequate prompt information[27, 28]. As we have mentioned before, alignment between the input image and the resulting generated report is the fundamental concern. Competitive results are demonstrated by RAGSemRad when compared to the state-of-the-art methods. 2 Related Work 2.1 Image caption Image captioning, which involves understanding a given image by generating a descriptive sentence, has been extensively researched in recent years[2, 30–35]. Progress in image captioning has outpaced that in report generation due to advancements in deep learning techniques and the availability of large-scale datasets. Traditional image captioning methods typically adopt an encoder-decoder architecture, where CNNs encode the image to derive corresponding representations, and RNNs coupled with attention mechanisms translate these representations into captions[2, 31, 33, 35]. Additionally, some studies have explored visual relationships among image regions by constructing scene graphs during the encoding phase[30, 34]. Given the limitations of RNNs in modeling long-range dependencies, Transformer-based models have been introduced in image captioning tasks[32, 34]. In contrast to image captioning, paragraph generation, a closely related task to report generation, focuses on producing detailed and semantically coherent paragraphs describing visual content. Hierarchical RNN structures are commonly employed in paragraph generation, where the decoding stage is divided into two steps: topic vector generation by a topic decoder and sentence generation by a sentence decoder. Concurrently, the advent of LLMs has spurred attempts by researchers to harness these models for the generation of textual paragraphs[36, 37], leveraging the contextual comprehension inherent in LLMs. Illustratively, Xie et al.[37] employed a substantial pre-trained multi-modal Xing Jia et al.: Semantic Feedback-Based RAG for Radiology Report Generation 395 model to derive visual cues from input images, which are then used to craft detailed paragraphs. 2.2 Radiology report generation Compared to image captioning and paragraph generation tasks, ensuring clinical accuracy in generated reports is the fundamental concern in the radiology report generation task. Most report generation models adhere to the encoder-decoder framework[1, 4–19, 38, 39], addressing differences between image captioning (or paragraph generation) and report generation. For example, Jing et al.[1] introduced a co- attention mechanism into report generation models to simultaneously explore visual and semantic information. Wang et al.[40] proposed a self-boosting framework that enhances report generation through collaboration between the primary task of report generation and an auxiliary task of image-text matching. Prior knowledge has been leveraged by modeling disease correlations using knowledge graphs, such as KG[19], PPKED[7], and RareGen[10]. Some studies have compiled template databases to incorporate patterned information, such as Hybrid[15] and R2Gen[11]. Others have addressed data bias issues through contrastive learning mechanisms[6] or curriculum learning[4]. Several studies endeavors have sought to incorporate background data, including diagnostic details like medical histories and patient- reported symptoms, to facilitate the generation of medical reports[41–43]. Furthermore, other studies have delved into addressing issues, such as semantic redundancy[39], the coherence of report content[18], and the integration of visual data from multiple perspectives[13], among other challenges. Yin et al.[39] proposed a topic-matching mechanism to mitigate semantic repetition issues. Xue et al.[18] introduced a recurrent report generation model to ensure semantic coherence between adjacent sentences. Image-label dataset: CheXpert. The image-label dataset we employed is CheXpert[55], a publicly available dataset containing 224 316 radiology X-ray images along with 14-dimensional clinical labels, which include annotations for conditions: Atelectasis, Cardiomegaly, Consolidation, Edema, Enlarged Cardiomediastinum, Fracture, Lung Lesion, Lung Opacity, No Finding, Pleural Effusion, Pleural Other, Pneumonia, Pneumothorax, and Support Devices. Image-report datasets: IU X-Ray and MIMIC- CXR. We utilize two benchmark datasets for report generation: IU X-Ray[56] and MIMIC-CXR[57]. IU X- Ray comprises 3955 reports and 7470 chest X-ray images from frontal and/or lateral views. Each study typically includes sections like impression, findings, comparison, and indication. For consistency with prior research[1, 7, 11], we concatenate the impression and findings sections as the target output and utilize multi- view chest X-ray images. MIMIC-CXR, the largest report generation dataset to date, comprises 377 110 chest X-ray images and 227 835 reports from 64 588 patients. The dataset includes images from various views, such as Anterior-Posterior (AP), Posterior- Anterior (PA), and LAteral (LA). Reports in MIMIC- CXR usually consist of multiple sections, like comparison, clinical history, indication, reasons for examination, impressions, and findings. Following the experimental setups in Ref. [9], we focus on generating text from the “findings” section as the medical report and utilize multi-view images. Consistent with previous studies[1, 7, 11], we split the image-report pairs randomly for training, validation, and testing sets of IU X-Ray with proportions of 0.8, 0.1, and 0.1, respectively. For MIMIC-CXR, we adopt the official split: 368 960 in the training set, 2991 in the validation set, and 5159 in the testing set. The image- label dataset is included in the training sets of IU X- Ray and MIMIC-CXR. All evaluations are conducted on the testing sets of IU X-Ray and MIMIC-CXR, separately. 4.2 Metrics Consistent with current research trends, we assess the efficacy by utilizing standard Natural Language Generation (NLG) evaluation metrics. These encompass BLEU-1, 2, 3, 4, and ROUGEL-L scores, which are broadly used to gauge the quality of text. Furthermore, our evaluation scope is broadened to incorporate a report classification model, specifically for determining the Clinical Effectiveness (CE) of the reports produced. The metrics for evaluating the classification model consist of Accuracy, F1-score, Precision, and Recall. In order to enhance the reliability of our findings and reduce the influence of limited sample sizes on individual class metrics, we utilize the micro-average method to compute the Precision, Recall, and F1-score metrics. 4.3 Model settings fcnn λ In our model setup, we utilize DenseNet 121[58] as the visual extractor for extracting visual features from input images, with the fully connected layers removed. For the image and text encoders, Multi-Head Attention (MHA) layer is employed, with the number of heads in MHA set to 3. To handle multi-label classification, we implement a weighted binary cross-entropy loss, transforming it into multiple binary classifications. We take the 3.55×108-parameter model GPT-2 Medium[59] as the decoder in this paper. Parameter optimization is carried out using the Adam optimizer with a batch size of 32 and a learning rate of 0.0001. Considering the average sentence count in a report, we select the top-7 sentences as the semantic text for each image. All implementations are executed using PyTorch and run on NVIDIA Tesla V100 GPUs.
